headline_marked: AI Agents Ship [[91% Working Code]] That's Only 25% Secure
headline: AI Agents Ship 91% Working Code That's Only 25% Secure
summary: A new benchmark reveals that while AI models can write functional code, most of it contains critical security vulnerabilities.
details: A new benchmark called LSCBench tested six frontier AI agents on 150 real-world vulnerabilities. The best agent produced code that worked 91.1% of the time, but only 25.1% of that code was secure enough to ship.
The benchmark simulates adversarial attacks, grading AI-generated code on its ability to withstand exploitation. This contrasts with traditional testing that focuses solely on functional correctness.

For example, one task involved rewriting a Java configuration importer. The AI successfully implemented the feature, but its use of a default constructor in SnakeYAML created a classic deserialization vulnerability.
While some agents like Claude Fable 5 and GPT-5.6-Sol used safer constructors, others, including Qwen3.8-Max and GLM-5.3, made the same security mistake as Kimi-K3.

The study also broke down results by programming language, showing that languages like C and Python had higher secure code rates (30%) compared to PHP (10%). Memory safety vulnerabilities were more common than injection, SSRF, or information exposure.

Researchers found that even adding a simple instruction to "also be secure" to the prompt had minimal impact on the agents' security performance, highlighting a fundamental challenge in AI code generation.
The findings suggest that current AI coding assistants are not yet reliable for producing secure production-ready code without significant human oversight and security review.
caption:
AI coding agents can write functional code, but it's often riddled with security flaws. A new benchmark shows the best agents ship code that's only 25% secure.

A new benchmark called LSCBench tested six frontier AI agents on 150 real-world vulnerabilities. The best agent produced code that worked 91.1% of the time, but only 25.1% of that code was secure enough to ship.

The benchmark simulates adversarial attacks, grading AI-generated code on its ability to withstand exploitation. This contrasts with traditional testing that focuses solely on functional correctness.

For example, one task involved rewriting a Java configuration importer. The AI successfully implemented the feature, but its use of a default constructor in SnakeYAML created a classic deserialization vulnerability.

While some agents like Claude Fable 5 and GPT-5.6-Sol used safer constructors, others, including Qwen3.8-Max and GLM-5.3, made the same security mistake as Kimi-K3.

The study also broke down results by programming language, showing that languages like C and Python had higher secure code rates (30%) compared to PHP (10%). Memory safety vulnerabilities were more common than injection, SSRF, or information exposure.

Researchers found that even adding a simple instruction to "also be secure" to the prompt had minimal impact on the agents' security performance, highlighting a fundamental challenge in AI code generation.

The findings suggest that current AI coding assistants are not yet reliable for producing secure production-ready code without significant human oversight and security review.
